progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: Stage 5 (assumed, not re-taught): all living things are made of cells, and a light microscope shows cells and a nucleus; bacteria are single-celled living things. Also used from Stage 5 (route stage5AssumedKnowledge): plant and animal cells have a nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane; DNA carries inherited information; cells respire. Not assumed: prokaryote, eukaryote, membrane-bound, nucleoid, organelle, plasmid, micrometre, nanometre, ribosome, 70S and 80S, micrograph, nuclear envelope.
progression.startsWith: Put a prepared, stained slide of cheek cells under a light microscope. You'll see big, flat cells, each with a dark dot near the middle. Look closely at their edges, and you might spot tiny specks stuck to them. Those specks are bacteria from your mouth. Both are alive, releasing energy and making proteins. Yet they're built in two completely different ways. So how do the two cell types differ, and how do we actually know?
progression.stopsAfter: defining eukaryote and prokaryote by whether the DNA is enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus; naming the shared features (cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA); comparing the two feature by feature (nucleus, DNA shape and plasmids, membrane-bound organelles, size about 1 to 5 µm against about 10 to 100 µm, 70S against 80S ribosomes); explaining why compartments matter and why "no organelles" is not "primitive"; stating that light microscopes show cells and nuclei but not internal membranes, that electron microscopes revealed that typical prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and that a comparison should cross-check micrographs, diagrams and measurements; writing a comparison as both cells on the same feature; classifying a described cell from evidence and judging a single schematic source.

teaching.task: *How do prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells differ, and how do we know?*
teaching.causalExplanation: One question splits every cell ever found into two groups: is the cell's DNA wrapped inside its own membrane? When a membrane surrounds something, we call that thing membrane-bound. In your cheek cell, the DNA sits inside a membrane-bound nucleus. That makes it a eukaryote. In the bacterium, there's no nucleus. Its DNA lies loose in the cytoplasm, in a region called the nucleoid. That makes it a prokaryote. All bacteria are prokaryotes. Animals, plants, fungi like yeast, and single-celled protists are built from eukaryotic cells. But here's the important part. Every cell, of either type, has the same basic kit: a cell membrane around it, cytoplasm, the jelly-like fluid inside, ribosomes, which build proteins, and DNA, which carries the instructions. So the difference isn't what's inside. It's how it's organised. Start with the DNA itself. A prokaryote usually has one circular chromosome, a single loop of DNA, lying in the nucleoid. Many also carry plasmids, small extra rings of DNA. A eukaryote has several long, straight chromosomes, and they're kept inside the nucleus, separated from the cytoplasm by the nuclear membrane, also called the nuclear envelope.

teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. An electron micrograph shows a cell three micrometres long. It has no nuclear envelope, ribosomes throughout its cytoplasm, and a single circular DNA molecule. Identify the cell type, and justify your answer using two pieces of evidence from the micrograph. Pause here to answer. Second. A textbook diagram shows a bacterium and a human cheek cell side by side, drawn the same size. A student concludes that the two cells are about the same size. Explain why this conclusion is not reliable, and name another source that could check it, saying what that source would show. Pause here to answer.
